Early
extension
Rule table: hips toward the ball over
4% of body height.
It may feel like you stay down, but at
impact your hips have moved toward
the ball.
Through the downswing your hips drift toward the ball instead of turning out of the way.
That leaves your arms with no room, so you stand up through impact to make space.
That is why the strike can come out thin or blocked. The likely reason is that your hips
do not rotate freely: your lead hip had only turned about 31° at impact. Work on the turn,
not on staying down. The wall drill trains your trail glute to stay back while you rotate,
and the 90/90 stretch gives the hips the range to do it.

text.tspan: Answers are based only on this analysis.
It will not add faults, numbers or drills.
Ask me anything about this result: the 7% hip
measurement, the fault chain, or the wall drill.
Why does it feel like I’m staying
down when I’m not?
Your chest stays over the ball, so it feels like
you stay down. But in your impact key frame
your backside is off the line it touched at
address: your hips are 7% of your body height
closer to the ball. That is the extension. The
wall drill gives you something you can check: if
your trail glute leaves the wall, you have
extended.
Is the hip rotation thing certain?
No. Restricted hip rotation is the likely cause,
not a measurement. It is pointed to by your
lead hip turning 31° at impact against about
45° typical, with medium confidence. A coach
can check it in person.
